title: Your Portfolio Does Not Owe You Rent
meta_description: Turn total portfolio return into sustainable spending without mistaking dividends, managed distributions or returned principal for a paycheck.

sections.heading: A Distribution Is Not a Paycheck
paragraphs: A portfolio can send cash every month and still be shrinking. The payment may come from dividends, bond interest, realized gains, option premiums, return of capital or the sale of shares. All arrive as spendable dollars, but they do not carry the same economic meaning. Calling every distribution income can make principal depletion look like yield.

Rent creates a useful but imperfect metaphor. A tenant pays for temporary use of an asset; a portfolio distribution transfers value already belonging to the investor. When a fund pays a distribution, its net asset value normally falls by the amount transferred, all else equal. [[S1|Investor.gov explains]] that distributions can come from dividends, interest, gains or return of capital and that total return is more informative than the distribution alone.

That does not make dividends fake or irrelevant. A profitable company may distribute part of its earnings, and bonds contractually pay interest subject to credit risk. The mistake is treating the cash payment as additional to the value of the security rather than part of the total return delivered by it.

A $1 dividend from a share that falls by roughly $1 on the ex-dividend date does not create a free dollar. The investor holds less market value and more cash. Subsequent price movement depends on many factors, but the accounting transfer should prevent yield from being confused with a separate layer of wealth.

The portfolio therefore does not owe the investor rent. The investor owns a changing pool of assets and needs a withdrawal policy that converts total return into spending. That policy can use natural income, selective sales, cash reserves and rebalancing. It should not force the portfolio into high-yield products merely to avoid selling shares.

A high displayed yield can coexist with falling principal, leverage, concentration or an unsustainable payout. A low-yield diversified portfolio can support withdrawals by combining dividends with planned sales. Judge the whole machine: return after costs and tax, volatility, inflation, withdrawal rate, time horizon and flexibility.

Start by separating three figures on the statement: cash distributed, change in market value and investor withdrawals. Reinvested income remains part of return; cash removed becomes spending. Only the combined total explains whether the account grew, held purchasing power or funded consumption by reducing assets.

This article builds a rent-like spending system without pretending the portfolio is a building. It distinguishes yield from total return, sizes withdrawals against goals, manages sequence risk, creates a cash calendar, coordinates taxes and reviews whether the plan remains sustainable.

The desired result is not the largest monthly payment. It is reliable spending with a portfolio capable of supporting later years. A smooth distribution that quietly returns principal is less dependable than a flexible plan that makes occasional, transparent sales.

Monthly-payment marketing can exploit the household's preference for salary-like regularity. Regularity is administratively useful, but it is not proof of safety. Ask whether the amount changes with markets, who may cut it, and whether principal supports it. A payment schedule is a delivery convention; sustainability comes from assets, returns and the withdrawal claim.

Keep the language precise with family members. Call dividends and interest investment income, call sales proceeds withdrawals, and call return of capital principal returned. The checking account may treat each dollar identically, but the plan should not. Clear labels prevent a temporary distribution policy from quietly becoming a permanent spending promise.

sections.heading: Follow the Cash to Its Source
paragraphs: Read each distribution's classification. Brokerage statements and tax forms may distinguish ordinary dividends, qualified dividends, interest, capital-gain distributions and nondividend distributions. The IRS's Publication 550 explains these categories and their reporting. [[S4|Tax labels matter]], but they do not by themselves determine whether a product is suitable.

Return of capital is especially easy to misunderstand. It can represent the fund returning part of the investor's own basis rather than earnings. It is not automatically fraud or evidence of poor management; some structures use it intentionally. Yet it reduces basis and can increase gain recognized later, while reducing assets available to compound.

Closed-end funds may follow managed distribution policies that pay a fixed amount even when current income is insufficient. Investor.gov warns that payments can include return of capital and that leverage can increase gains, losses and price volatility. [[S2|The fund bulletin]] recommends understanding source, fees, leverage and market-price discounts or premiums.

Covered-call and option-income strategies convert some potential upside into current premium and introduce option-specific outcomes. The payout is not equivalent to bond interest, and a large distribution does not state total return. Compare the strategy with an appropriate benchmark through rising, falling and sideways markets, net of fees and taxes.

Bond income carries interest-rate, inflation, reinvestment and credit risks. A high yield may compensate for a real probability of default or price loss. If rates fall, maturing cash may reinvest at lower yields; if rates rise, existing bond prices can decline. Match maturity and quality to the spending horizon rather than buying the highest quoted yield.

Real-estate investment trusts and business-development companies can distribute substantial cash under their structures, but assets, leverage and sector concentration remain relevant. A payout sourced from rent or loan interest still depends on tenants, borrowers, valuations, financing and management. Diversify by economic risk, not by the number of ticker symbols.

Fund distribution rates are often calculated from recent payments and market price. They are not promises. A falling share price can make a historical distribution look like a higher current yield immediately before a cut. Use standardized yield, total return, coverage information and official reports where available.

Reinvested distributions can create a misleading tax surprise in taxable accounts. Investor.gov notes that fund capital gains, interest and dividends may be taxable even when reinvested. Keep a tax reserve and cost-basis records rather than assuming no cash withdrawal means no current tax.

Build an income-source table for every holding: expected payment, legal source, variability, fees, tax treatment, concentration and conditions for reduction. If the source cannot be explained without marketing language, the payment should not be used as the foundation for essential spending.

Read distribution notices over several periods, not one year-end form. The source can change as markets and realized gains change. A fund that covered payments from gains in a strong year may use returned capital in a weak one. Compare cumulative distributions with cumulative total return and ending assets instead of treating each payment as independent success.

Consider what the issuer retains. A company that pays less may reinvest profit at attractive returns, repay debt or preserve resilience; another may distribute heavily because growth options are limited. Neither policy is automatically superior. The investor should own businesses and funds for risk-adjusted total return, not force every holding to mimic an employer payroll department.

sections.heading: Use Total Return to Fund the Rent
paragraphs: Total return combines income distributions and change in value over a period, assuming appropriate treatment of reinvestment. It is the correct starting lens for comparing a growth-heavy fund with an income-heavy fund. Distribution yield alone rewards products for moving value into cash, even when the investor could create cash by selling a small number of shares.

A total-return withdrawal policy starts with the household's spending gap after dependable income such as wages, pension or Social Security. The portfolio funds the gap, not an arbitrary yield target. If the gap is $24,000, the relevant questions are whether the assets, horizon, risk and flexibility can support $24,000—not which product advertises exactly $2,000 monthly.

Natural dividends and interest can collect in the settlement account. The remaining gap can be funded through periodic sales chosen as part of rebalancing. Selling shares is not inherently more destructive than receiving a distribution; both reduce the value remaining in the account by the cash removed, before subsequent returns and taxes.

Use a withdrawal calendar. Estimate twelve months of essential and discretionary spending, map outside income, tax dates and irregular bills, then schedule portfolio transfers quarterly or monthly. The account need not produce cash on the same day rent or a mortgage is due if a separate spending account holds the next period's needs.

Avoid changing the strategic portfolio merely to match the calendar. A monthly payer is not automatically safer than a quarterly payer, and a high-dividend portfolio is not automatically less volatile than a broad portfolio. The bank account can smooth timing while investments retain their intended allocation.

Fees belong in the gap. Advisory fees, fund expenses, trading costs, bid-ask spreads and product charges reduce assets supporting future spending. A strategy that advertises 7 percent distributions but costs more and delivers weaker total return may provide less sustainable income than a lower-cost diversified approach.

Inflation converts nominal comfort into future pressure. A fixed $2,000 monthly payment loses purchasing power over a long retirement. Growth assets can help address inflation but add volatility. The plan needs both near-term spending stability and long-term capacity rather than treating current yield as permanent real income.

Compare withdrawals with portfolio value at a consistent review date, not after every market move. A trailing twelve-month withdrawal rate and multi-year total-return record reveal more than one distribution. Explain changes from market return, contributions, withdrawals, fees and tax separately.

Total return does not guarantee sustainability. A strong past return can reverse, and average return ignores order. The advantage of the framework is honesty: it labels spending as a claim on the entire portfolio and makes the required trade-offs visible.

Use sales as part of a written rebalancing order. Sell overweight assets or direct new income away from them, while considering tax lots and transaction costs. This avoids a habit of liquidating whichever holding feels least emotionally important. The cash decision and allocation decision should be solved together.

A total-return approach also clarifies benchmarking. Compare the portfolio after all distributions are assumed reinvested, then subtract household withdrawals separately. Otherwise a high-distribution fund can appear to fall while a growth fund appears to rise simply because value was delivered in different forms. Consistent measurement makes the comparison meaningful.

sections.heading: Sequence Risk Changes the Same Average
paragraphs: Two retirees can earn the same long-run average return and experience different outcomes if withdrawals occur in a different order. Poor returns early force more shares to be sold when prices are low, leaving fewer assets for a later recovery. This is sequence-of-returns risk, and it becomes material when withdrawals begin.

The risk is not solved by owning dividend stocks. Dividends can be cut, prices can fall and a concentrated income portfolio can suffer sector-specific damage. A company choosing to distribute cash does not immunize the investor from market value, inflation or business risk.

Vanguard illustrates the issue with historical retirement examples and supports spending flexibility. Its research describes dynamic spending as adjusting withdrawals within a ceiling and floor after market changes. [[S3|The strategy]] aims to balance current spending with portfolio viability; it is not a guarantee and the appropriate boundaries depend on the household.

Separate essential and discretionary spending. Housing, food, insurance, health and minimum obligations require stronger funding than travel, gifts or upgrades. Dependable income, cash or high-quality near-term assets can cover more of the essential floor, while discretionary portfolio withdrawals can absorb larger adjustments after bad markets.

A temporary reduction can have a disproportionate benefit because it avoids selling as much after a decline. Options include pausing inflation increases, reducing discretionary travel, delaying a large gift or using other income. Flexibility should be designed before the decline, not improvised after fear and family expectations harden.

Do not let flexibility become an excuse for an unrealistic initial rate. A ceiling and floor moderate changes; they do not create assets. Test longer life, weak early returns, inflation, fees, taxes and major care costs. The plan should identify which spending changes happen at predetermined portfolio thresholds.

A balanced allocation may reduce volatility relative to all equities, but bonds also lose value and face inflation or credit risk. Asset allocation follows horizon, spending floor and capacity for loss. The goal is not to eliminate sequence risk but to avoid combining high withdrawals with an allocation that cannot withstand early stress.

Rehearse a 20 percent and 30 percent portfolio decline. Calculate the new withdrawal percentage, the cash runway and which discretionary items change. If the result is unacceptable, adjust the rate, allocation or spending before retirement rather than relying on dividends to make the decline feel less real.

Review after major market and life changes, but avoid rewriting the plan every week. Sequence defenses are rules—cash segmentation, rebalancing and bounded spending changes—not forecasts about the next recovery date.

Longevity and sequence interact. A longer horizon creates more years for recovery but also more withdrawals and inflation. Do not assume conservative spending in the first decade solves every later risk. Revisit health, housing, care, survivor income and estate priorities as the household changes, and distinguish flexible lifestyle goals from obligations that cannot be cut.

Poor sequences can also occur outside a famous crash through several mediocre years combined with high inflation. Stress tests should include dull disappointment, not only a dramatic one-year fall. A plan that survives because it assumes an immediate rebound may still be fragile when purchasing power erodes gradually and the recovery arrives late.

sections.heading: Build a Spending Buffer, Not a Cash Fortress
paragraphs: A spending buffer separates the bill-paying calendar from daily markets. It may hold several months of planned withdrawals in insured deposits, Treasury bills, a money market fund or other appropriate short-term assets. Product choice depends on protection, access, maturity, tax and risk; similarly named bank and mutual-fund products do not have identical insurance.

The buffer is not free protection. Cash and very short-term assets can lag inflation and long-term portfolio returns. Holding many years of spending may reduce growth enough to create another sustainability problem. Choose the amount from dependable income, flexibility, account structure and tolerance for selling during declines.

Refill by rule. Dividends and interest can flow to the buffer, and periodic rebalancing can top it up after strong asset performance. During a decline, the household can spend the buffer temporarily rather than selling the most depressed assets, then restore it when the portfolio or income plan permits.

Do not describe the buffer as preventing losses. It changes timing and behavior; it cannot guarantee that markets recover before the buffer empties. Long declines, inflation and unexpected expenses can consume it. The strategic allocation and withdrawal rate remain the core drivers.

Keep emergency savings separate. Emergency funds cover unplanned shocks; the spending buffer contains planned portfolio withdrawals. Combining them can cause ordinary spending to consume protection needed for health, home or family disruptions. Label both and establish which is replenished first.

Match maturities to the calendar. Treasury or CD ladders can release cash across known periods, but early-sale prices and penalties matter. Keep the nearest bills accessible and avoid a maturity schedule so complicated that a missed action causes an overdraft.

Understand money market funds. Investor.gov says they invest in short-term debt and historically have lower risk than many funds, but they are securities, not FDIC-insured bank deposits, and can face losses or liquidity tools. [[S6|Read the fund's category and terms]] rather than treating every cash-like balance as identical.

Automate transfers from the buffer to checking at a sustainable amount. Automation smooths administration, but quarterly review should compare the scheduled transfer with actual spending and portfolio value. Increasing the automatic payment after a strong month can turn lifestyle inflation into a permanent claim.
The ideal buffer makes markets less relevant to next month's bills without making long-term growth irrelevant to later decades. Its size is a compromise, not a badge of conservatism.

Hold the buffer in accounts whose operational details are understood. Settlement, bank-transfer cutoffs, weekends and withdrawal restrictions can matter when bills are automated. Test a small transfer and document which account funds which month. A buffer visible only inside a brokerage interface is not complete until the route to checking works.

Refilling should respect valuation rather than emotion. After strong returns, restore the target buffer and allocation according to policy; after weak returns, use the planned runway and spending adjustments. Constantly enlarging cash because markets feel dangerous can lock in an allocation change without acknowledging its growth and inflation costs.

sections.heading: Taxes Decide Which Dollar Arrives
paragraphs: Gross distribution is not spendable income after tax. Interest, ordinary dividends, qualified dividends, capital-gain distributions, realized gains and retirement-account withdrawals can receive different treatment. State rules and income interactions add complexity. Build the spending plan from estimated after-tax cash.

IRS Publication 550 covers investment income, qualified and ordinary dividends, nondividend distributions, gains, losses and basis. [[S4|The publication]] shows why the form of a payment matters. Tax law changes and individual facts can require professional advice; the portfolio should not rely on a simplified internet rate.

Account location changes withdrawal consequences. Traditional retirement-account distributions are generally taxable under applicable rules; qualified Roth withdrawals may receive different treatment; taxable accounts create basis and gain calculations. Required minimum distributions can affect timing for some owners. Coordinate rather than draining whichever account displays the most cash.

A tax-smart sequence often uses multiple account types across years, but there is no universal order. Current and future tax brackets, Social Security, health-premium thresholds, estate plans, charitable giving and heirs can change the answer. Model several years instead of minimizing this year's bill in isolation.

Withholding and estimated payments belong on the cash calendar. A large distribution with no withholding can create an April surprise or penalty. Keep tax cash separate from spending and reconcile forms with statements. Reinvested taxable distributions may require payment even though the account produced no spendable cash.

Selling shares allows tax-lot selection in taxable accounts. Specific identification may realize different gains or losses, subject to records and broker procedures. Tax-loss harvesting can help in some circumstances, but wash-sale rules and portfolio exposure matter. A tax tactic should not distort the strategic allocation.

Return of capital can defer current tax by reducing basis, but later gain may rise. A product advertising tax-advantaged distributions may be handing back principal. Review tax forms and notices rather than assuming the payment was earned yield.

Fees and taxes should be reported together with withdrawals. A household withdrawing 4 percent while another 1 percent leaves through costs and taxes places a different claim on assets than the headline spending rate suggests. Track all portfolio outflows.

Tax efficiency improves a viable withdrawal policy; it cannot make an excessive rate safe. Start with sustainable gross economics, then choose account and transaction tactics that deliver more of the same total return to the household.

Plan for surviving spouses and incapacity. Account ownership, beneficiary designation and tax character can change after death, and one spouse may not understand the current withdrawal order. Keep a plain-language map of accounts, expected forms and professional contacts. Tax optimization that cannot be operated by the household is not operationally sound.

Estimate taxes as a range until actual income is known. Capital gains, deductions, withholding and other income can move the final liability. Update during the year after large sales or conversions rather than discovering the gap at filing. The spending transfer should remain net of a tax reserve that is visibly separate.

sections.heading: Do Not Buy Yield to Fix a Spending Gap
paragraphs: A spending gap creates temptation to reverse-engineer yield. If the household needs 8 percent, an 8-percent product appears to solve the problem without selling principal. But the required cash does not determine what markets can safely provide. Higher yields usually arrive with credit, leverage, concentration, option, liquidity or principal risk.

Inspect any product whose distribution seems calibrated to the household's need. Ask whether the payout is covered by income, realized gains or return of capital; whether leverage is used; how fees compare; and how market price behaves. Read official filings and distribution notices, not only the headline yield.

Diversification can be lost gradually. A basket of high-yield stocks may concentrate in utilities, energy, financials or real estate. Several option-income funds may own the same large companies. Map underlying economic exposures and compare them with the household's employment, property and pension risks.

Dividend cuts are not investor failure. Companies preserve cash when conditions or capital needs change. A plan that cannot tolerate a cut has treated a board decision as a salary contract. Use a diversified total-return framework and a buffer rather than requiring each holding to maintain its payment.

Avoid borrowing against the portfolio to preserve distributions. Margin or securities-backed loans add interest and collateral calls; a market decline can force sales at the wrong time. Debt can transform a spending problem into a solvency problem while creating the illusion that principal remains untouched.

Annuities and other guaranteed-income products can transfer some longevity or market risk under contract, but guarantees depend on terms and insurer claims-paying ability, and liquidity, fees and inflation protection vary. Compare them for the essential-income job rather than treating every product labeled income as equivalent.

The honest solutions to an oversized gap are limited: spend less, earn longer, delay the start, add dependable income, contribute more, adjust goals or accept carefully evaluated risk. A product cannot erase arithmetic merely by paying monthly.

Measure yield on cost only for historical curiosity. The relevant decision uses current value, future cash and alternative risk. A stock bought cheaply years ago does not produce free income today; keeping it commits its current market value to that risk.

Reject the emotional rule that selling shares means failure. Planned sales can be the cleanest way to convert a diversified portfolio into cash. The failure is taking an unsustainable amount while hiding it behind a distribution label.

When evaluating a yield increase, ask what new risk was accepted per dollar of additional cash. A move from diversified equities to a concentrated high-dividend sector may reduce growth and increase one economic exposure. A move to lower-quality credit may make the payment more vulnerable in the same recession that pressures household finances.

Do not confuse historical payment streaks with a legal guarantee. Management and boards respond to business conditions, and funds can revise policies. A durable household plan assumes some income sources will disappoint and uses diversification, reserves and spending flexibility rather than requiring every issuer to preserve the investor's preferred calendar.

sections.heading: Run the Annual Portfolio Paycheck Audit
paragraphs: Once a year, calculate all dependable nonportfolio income, essential spending, discretionary spending and tax. The difference is the portfolio claim. Divide trailing withdrawals and portfolio-paid fees by a consistent beginning or average balance, then compare with the plan and time horizon. Do not wait for the account to decline before measuring.

Attribute total return: dividends, interest, realized and unrealized gains, fees, tax and withdrawals. Confirm whether distributions include return of capital. Compare each fund with an appropriate total-return benchmark and examine risk, not merely payout consistency.

Review the allocation after withdrawals. Selling only growth assets to preserve dividend holdings can distort diversification, while spending every bond payment can shift the portfolio toward equities. Rebalance the entire household portfolio, including retirement, taxable and cash accounts, according to the policy.

Update the spending calendar and buffer. Record irregular bills, planned gifts, travel, taxes and large replacements. Decide the next year's transfer amount and the conditions for a cut or increase. A written ceiling and floor reduce negotiation after every market move.

Stress three cases: early bear market, persistent inflation and unexpectedly long life. Add care or housing costs relevant to the household. Identify which expenses change, which assets fund the first years and when outside advice or a plan reset is triggered.

Check beneficiaries, account access, fraud controls and the person who can act after incapacity. A withdrawal strategy that only one person understands is operationally fragile. Keep a concise investment policy and cash map without exposing passwords insecurely.

Review products that became more complex than their job requires. High fees, leverage, discounts, tax surprises or opaque distributions should earn their place with measurable benefit. Simplicity can improve monitoring and reduce the chance that a steady payment conceals principal erosion.

Coordinate with qualified tax and financial professionals where stakes or complexity justify it, while understanding assumptions and conflicts. No simulation certifies the future. The review should produce ranges, decision rules and ownership rather than a single guaranteed outcome.

A portfolio can help pay the rent without becoming a rent-paying machine. Total return creates the resources; a withdrawal policy converts them; a buffer handles timing; taxes and fees determine delivery; and flexibility protects later years. The paycheck is designed by the household, not promised by the distribution yield.

The audit should preserve last year's forecasts beside actual results. Record planned and actual spending, tax, distributions, sales, fees and ending allocation. Variances reveal whether the household underestimated lifestyle, whether products changed payment source or whether market gains masked excessive withdrawals. Without the comparison, a rising balance can excuse weak discipline until conditions reverse.

Finish with three decisions at most: next year's transfer, allocation trades and one risk-control improvement. A complex report that produces no ownership or date will not guide the next withdrawal. The purpose of the audit is to convert uncertain markets into a small set of actions the household can repeat without chasing yield or reacting to every statement.

summary: A portfolio distribution is not automatically income in the economic sense. It may come from dividends, interest, realized gains, option premiums, return of capital or share sales. When a fund distributes value, its net asset value normally falls by the amount transferred, all else equal. Evaluate total return—income plus changes in value—rather than treating the payout as an extra layer of wealth.

Build spending from the household gap. Subtract dependable wages, pension, Social Security or other income from planned after-tax spending. The portfolio funds the difference using natural income and planned sales. It does not need a product whose advertised yield exactly matches the gap. A high-yield portfolio can shrink, while a diversified lower-yield portfolio can provide cash through transparent rebalancing sales.

Trace every distribution. Closed-end funds and other vehicles may use managed distribution policies that include return of capital. Bond yields compensate for interest-rate, credit, inflation and reinvestment risks. Option-income, REIT and business-development-company payouts have their own exposures. Review coverage, leverage, fees, custody, tax classification and total return rather than comparing headline yield alone.

Sequence risk means the order of returns matters after withdrawals begin. Poor early markets can force the sale of more shares and leave fewer assets for recovery even when long-run average return later looks acceptable. Separate essential from discretionary spending and predefine bounded reductions after weak markets. Dynamic spending with a ceiling and floor can add flexibility, but it cannot rescue an excessive initial claim.

A spending buffer can hold upcoming planned withdrawals in suitable cash or short-term assets so next month's bills do not require a market trade. It is separate from the emergency fund and needs a refill rule. The buffer changes timing; it does not guarantee that markets recover before it runs out. Too much cash can create inflation and opportunity costs, so size it from the household's income stability and flexibility.

Taxes determine how much reaches checking. Interest, qualified and ordinary dividends, capital-gain distributions, nondividend distributions, realized gains and retirement withdrawals can be treated differently. Coordinate taxable, tax-deferred and Roth-type accounts across years, maintain basis records, reserve for taxes and track portfolio fees and tax outflows alongside household withdrawals.

Do not buy yield merely because spending is high. A required 8-percent cash flow does not create a safe 8-percent investment. Large payouts often bring leverage, concentration, credit, liquidity, option or principal risk. Honest remedies include lower spending, longer work, delayed withdrawals, more dependable income, additional saving or carefully evaluated changes in risk—not a distribution label.

Audit annually. Calculate the portfolio claim, attribute total return, check for return of capital, restore the strategic allocation, update the cash calendar and stress early losses, inflation and longevity. Set next year's transfer with explicit conditions for increases and reductions. A portfolio can pay household bills, but the paycheck comes from a disciplined total-return withdrawal policy—not from the fiction that investments owe monthly rent.

Keep measurement consistent. Compare investments on total return with distributions reinvested, then show household withdrawals, fees and portfolio-paid tax separately. Review distribution notices and tax forms for returned principal. Preserve the original annual forecast beside actual spending so a strong market cannot conceal an excessive claim. Regular monthly cash is useful for administration, but payment frequency is not evidence of safety or performance.

The final design has four layers: dependable outside income for part of the spending floor, a diversified portfolio aligned with horizon and risk, a short-term buffer for bill timing, and rules that adjust discretionary withdrawals after stress. No layer guarantees success. Together they make the trade-offs visible and reduce pressure to buy opaque high-yield products simply because the household prefers a salary-shaped payment.

faq.question: Are dividends free money?
faq.answer: No. A dividend transfers company value to shareholders, and market price generally adjusts around the ex-dividend date. It remains a valid part of total return.

faq.question: Is selling shares worse than spending dividends?
faq.answer: Not inherently. Both remove value from the portfolio. Planned sales can fund spending while preserving diversification and rebalancing.

faq.question: What is return of capital?
faq.answer: A distribution that returns part of the investor’s principal or basis rather than current earnings. It can reduce basis and future compounding assets.

faq.question: How much can I withdraw safely?
faq.answer: No percentage works for everyone. Horizon, allocation, fees, tax, inflation, sequence risk, outside income and spending flexibility all matter.

faq.question: Why keep a spending buffer?
faq.answer: It separates near-term bills from daily markets. The buffer needs a refill rule and should remain distinct from emergency savings.

faq.question: Should I buy the highest-yielding fund?
faq.answer: No. High yield can reflect leverage, credit risk, options, concentration, falling price or returned capital. Compare total return, risk, fees and taxes.

glossary.definition: Income distributions plus change in investment value over a period.
Recent or annualized distributions divided by a stated market value or price.
A distribution of the investor’s own principal or basis rather than current earnings.
The risk that poor returns early in withdrawals cause disproportionate long-term damage.
A withdrawal approach that adjusts spending within predefined limits as portfolio value changes.
The tax investment in an asset after applicable adjustments.
A dividend meeting tax-law requirements for potentially preferential federal rates.
Trading to restore a portfolio’s intended asset allocation.
Short-term assets reserved for planned portfolio withdrawals and bill timing.
A fund policy targeting regular payments that may come from income, gains or returned capital.
